text:
A reader who attends to what is missing will be repaid. Sarah does not appear anywhere in the chapter, and her death is announced in the verse that immediately follows it; the scene implies, though it never states, that something in the household did not survive the mountain. The narrator turns away at the very moment when a lesser storyteller would linger, and his silence is itself a kind of testimony. Abraham returns to the servants, and Isaac is not mentioned.

It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. Perhaps, in some sense, there is truth in this. But the same narrator tells us elsewhere what his characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence of chapter 22 is deliberate, and the narrator knows what he is about; in his voice, restraint is a kind of accusation.
